blocks.text: V. The last passage is Zechariah, chapter 5, verse 9, where the Prophet sees in a prophetic vision two women flying between heaven and earth, ורוח בכנפיהם ולהנה כנפים ככנפי החסידה, who had wind in their wings, and their wings were like the wings of the hasida, that is, of the stork. For why should I not translate it so? I do not now inquire what those two women signify, because the matter is full of obscurities and not necessary in this place. I assert only that by wings full of wind are meant here wings supremely well equipped for flight. Such are the wings of storks, with which they migrate to and return from very remote places, though places not well enough known. Pliny ^{e)}: From what place they come, or where they betake themselves, is still undiscovered. That they come from far away is not in doubt. Oppian in the Ixeutica: Whence they come and whither they return is not well established. Some say they fly from Lycia, others from Ethiopia. This seems capable of confirmation from the story we touched on above ^{f)} about a ginger root, still fresh, brought into Germany by a stork. For ginger grows mostly in Ethiopia, or, what is the same, Troglodytic Arabia. Dioscorides, book 1: Ζιγγίβερις ἴδιόν ἐστι φυτὸν, γεννώμενον ἐν τῇ Τρωγλοδυτικῇ Ἀραβίᾳ πλεῖστον [Zingiberis idion esti phyton, gennōmenon en tē Trōglodytikē Arabia pleiston]. Pliny, book 12, chapter 7, on pepper: The root of this tree is not, as some have supposed, what they call zimpiberi, and others zingiberi, although it is similar in taste. For that grows in Arabia and Troglodytica, on farms. Nor did Galen mean anything else when he wrote in book 6 of the Simples that ginger is imported from Barbaria. For Ethiopian Barbaria is meant, of which we spoke above ^{g)}. It must be admitted, meanwhile, that various places of India, such as Malabar, Bengala, Babul, Becain, are productive of ginger, as travellers testify, and that it is also found in the Omanitis of [col. 333] Arabia Felix. For so Abuchanipha: زنجبيل هو مما ينبت في بلاد العرب في الارض عمان [zanjabīl huwa mimmā yanbutu fī bilād al-ʿarab fī al-arḍ ʿumān] Ginger is among the things that grow in Arabia, in the land of Oman. But wherever ginger grows, from there to Germany [III, 94] is an immense journey, with much sea lying between, which storks would not cross unless they were exceedingly strong of wing ^{(4)}.
